Primary lymphocytic: **lichen planopilaris, frontal fibrosing alopecia (FFA), DLE, CCCA**; neutrophilic: **folliculitis decalvans**.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia** permanently destroys follicles. Primary types target the follicle (lymphocytic: LPP, FFA, DLE, CCCA; neutrophilic: folliculitis decalvans). Secondary scarring follows burns, trauma, tumours, kerion or long-standing traction.

Contrast with non-scarring loss ([alopecia areata](condition:alopecia-areata), [telogen effluvium](condition:telogen-effluvium), [androgenetic alopecia](condition:androgenetic-alopecia)) where ostia remain.

ul: Lymphocytic attack (LPP/FFA/DLE/CCCA) or neutrophilic folliculitis (FD, often *S. aureus*).
FFA incidence is rising, mainly in post-menopausal women.
CCCA predominantly affects women of African descent; hair practices contribute alongside genetics.
**"It will grow back like other hair loss"**: scarring loss is permanent; early treatment saves the rest.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Inflammation attacks the **follicle stem-cell bulge**, so the follicle can't regrow.

mech.t: Lymphocytes or neutrophils target the upper follicle, where stem cells live.
Without stem cells the follicle can't cycle.
The follicle is replaced by a fibrous tract and its opening disappears.
mech.caption: Inflammation around the upper follicle destroys it, leaving a fibrous tract.

mech.t: The skin loses openings and becomes smooth.

head: Clue
Non-scarring
Scarring
rows: Perifollicular erythema, scale, plugs, pustules, tufting

ul: **LPP:** white patches with spiky perifollicular scale; check mouth/skin LP.
**FFA:** frontal/temporal recession, lonely hairs, eyebrow loss, “unsunned” forehead band.
**DLE:** red scaly plugged plaques → dyspigmented scars; ears/face; ask lupus systemic features.
**FD:** pustules, crusts, doll’s-hair tufting at the vertex — swab.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical + trichoscopy (absent ostia). Specialist biopsy from the **active inflamed margin**. Primary care: good photos (clinical + dermoscopy if available), swab pustules, mycology if scale.

ddx.name: Kerion
ddx.f: Boggy child scalp infection — can scar; start antifungal pathway; do not incise

ul: **Urgent dermatology / Advice & Guidance** with photos (PCDS: scarring alopecia needs early referral).
While waiting: swab, mycology if indicated; baseline FBC, ferritin, U&E/LFT, TFT, vitamin D; ANA if lupus suspected; syphilis serology if indicated.
Do not delay referral for blood results.
Dermatologist may suggest potent topical steroid via A&G for symptoms.
Specialist ladders (awareness only): hydroxychloroquine, doxycycline, anti-androgens (FFA), systemic immunosuppressants, culture-guided antibiotics for FD — not routine IP initiation.

refer.t: Any loss of ostia, symptomatic inflamed edge, FFA pattern, CCCA pattern, lupus features, kerion, or uncertain “AA that will not regrow”.
Ulcerated/bleeding lesion on bald scalp → suspected-cancer pathway.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Any loss of ostia, symptomatic inflamed edge, FFA pattern, CCCA pattern, lupus features, kerion, or uncertain “AA that will not regrow”.
Ulcerated/bleeding lesion on bald scalp → suspected-cancer pathway.
Treatment slows or stops progression; lost hair doesn't return.

pearls: Side-by-side teaching: yellow dots (AA) vs absent ostia (scar).
FFA is often dismissed as “just ageing” — check brows and the frontal band.
Once scarred, the goal is halt progression, not regrowth.

quiz.q: When should you think of Scarring alopecia overview?
quiz.a: Shiny bald patch without follicular openings, often with itch, burning, perifollicular scale or pustules at the active edge.
Inflammation destroys the stem-cell bulge → fibrosis replaces the follicle.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Photograph, swab/mycology if pus or scale, baseline bloods, Advice & Guidance / urgent dermatology — do not watch and wait for “AA to regrow”.
Scarring alopecia is irreversible once established. Also refer non-healing nodules on bald scalp via suspected-cancer pathways.
